big: Meena sells a plot and receives ₹30 lakh in one go. The question is not what to buy. It is how to walk it into the market.

lines: I have ₹30 lakh from the plot. If I put it all in today and the market falls next week, I will never forgive myself.
That fear is common, and it is a reason to choose a method. One method is the STP. Let us watch it work.

alt: Money moving from a liquid fund jar to an equity fund jar each month
caps: All ₹30 lakh starts in a calm liquid fund.
Every month ₹2.5 lakh moves across to the equity fund.
The money still waiting keeps earning a small return.
After twelve months it has all moved. At an assumed 6% a year, the waiting money earned about ₹97,500.

title: What an STP does
stops: Beats a lump sum when markets rise
alt: A shield with four statements, two true and two false
caps: An STP is a way to enter, not a shield for the market.
It earns on the waiting money and softens the regret of one bad day.
But if markets rise straight away, the lump sum wins. And the equity part is still equity.

q: Meena has ₹30 lakh and is afraid of a fall just after she invests. Which plan fits her fear best?
opts: Put all of it into equity today, so that no single day of gains is missed
Hold it in a liquid fund and move it to equity in monthly steps with an STP
Start an SIP for the full ₹30 lakh from her bank account in the first month
Keep it in a savings account until the market looks cheap enough to enter
why: A lump sum is a fair choice for someone who can sit through a fall. Meena has said she cannot, so it is a poor fit.
An STP gives her a fixed entry plan, earns something while the money waits, and cuts the regret of a single bad entry day.
An SIP is built from regular income. It cannot be used to invest a sum already in hand, because the mandate is a few thousand rupees.
Waiting for a cheap market is a timing guess. The money earns little, and 'cheap' is clear only afterwards.

q: A market rise of 15% arrives in the month after Meena starts her 12-month STP. How does she compare with someone who invested the whole ₹30 lakh that day?
opts: She earns more, because the STP buys the units at lower prices than the lump sum did
She earns the same, because both of them put the same money in on the same day
She earns less this time, as most of her money was still in the liquid fund
She loses money, because an STP cannot make a gain when the market is rising
why: The STP buys at whatever the price is each month. In a market that only rises it buys at higher prices, not lower.
The two do not put the same money in at the same time. Most of her money was still in the liquid fund as the market rose.
A rising market rewards money that was already invested. She trades some of that gain for a smoother entry.
She still gains on the part moved over, plus interest on the rest. The STP does not stop gains, it only delays some.

q: What is the usual choice for the 'from' fund in an STP?
opts: A sector fund with a high-growth theme
A liquid or short-duration debt fund
A fund with a high exit load
why: A sector fund moves a lot. The waiting money should be calm, otherwise the parking spot is as risky as the destination.
These funds hold the money steadily and can be redeemed quickly, which suits money that moves out on a schedule.
An exit load would take a cut on each monthly transfer. The parking fund should charge little to leave.
Gold can swing in price and does not give the steady, small return that waiting money should earn.

q: Which statement about lump sum, SIP and STP is honest?
opts: The STP is the best method in every market
A lump sum always beats an SIP because more money works from day one
The best method is the one the investor can follow without panic
An SIP removes the risk that markets fall
why: In rising markets the lump sum can win. No method wins every time, so 'always the best' is a false promise.
Lump sums win when markets rise soon and lose when they fall. 'Always' is wrong in both directions.
A plan the investor sticks with beats a better plan that is dropped halfway. Match the method to the person.
An SIP spreads out the price you pay, but it does not stop the market from falling or protect against loss.

pts: Lump sum goes in at once. SIP spreads new savings. STP walks a lump sum from debt to equity.
An STP earns on the waiting money, but it can lag a lump sum in a rising market.
Choose the method the client can stick to.
